input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-532: Introduction to Intelligent Security Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: The course will introduce students to the application of intelligent methodologies in computer security and information assurance systems design. It will review different application areas such as intrusion detection and monitoring systems, access control and biological authentication, firewall structure and design. The students will be required to implement a course project on design of a particular security tool with an application of an artificial intelligence methodology and to undertake its performance analysis. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-735. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or CSCI-351 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-532]
The course will introduce students to the application of intelligent methodologies in computer security and information assurance systems design. It will review different application areas such as intrusion detection and monitoring systems, access control and biological authentication, firewall structure and design. The students will be required to implement a course project on design of a particular security tool with an application of an artificial intelligence methodology and to undertake its performance analysis. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-735. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or CSCI-351 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage to structure AI risk handling in security systems.
beats.example: Govern establishes policies for AI risk, Map documents context and intended use, Measure analyzes risks, and Manage prioritizes responses.
beats.title: Course Foundations and Framework Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a four-quadrant diagram labeled Govern, Map, Measure, Manage with brief icons representing policy, context, metrics, and response.

beats.claim: The Govern phase establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk within intelligent security systems.
beats.example: Institutional AI governance policies define who is accountable for security tool deployment and risk mitigation.
beats.title: Govern Phase and Accountability
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart starting with 'Govern' branching to 'Policy', 'Responsibility', and 'Accountability' nodes.

beats.claim: The Map phase documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts to inform AI risk assessment.
beats.example: Mapping a biometric authentication system requires documenting user demographics, intended access levels, and privacy impacts.
beats.title: Map Phase and Context Documentation
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a context-mapping template with fields for 'Context', 'Intended Use', 'Affected People', and 'Potential Impacts'.

beats.claim: The Measure phase uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks, considering data quality and uncertainty.
beats.example: Quantitative metrics like false positive rates and qualitative reviews of model bias are used to measure AI security tool risks.
beats.title: Measure Phase and Risk Analysis
beats.visualDirection: Display a split graphic showing 'Qualitative Methods' (checklists, reviews) and 'Quantitative Methods' (graphs, metrics).

beats.claim: The Manage phase prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring, continuing after deployment because context and system behavior can change.
beats.example: Post-deployment monitoring of an AI firewall detects distribution shift and triggers resource reallocation for updated threat models.
beats.title: Manage Phase and Post-Deployment Monitoring
beats.visualDirection: Render a circular lifecycle diagram with 'Manage' feeding back into 'Map' and 'Measure' to show continuous monitoring.

beats.claim: Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels.
beats.example: Supervised learning trains an intrusion detection system on labeled attack logs, whereas unsupervised learning clusters network traffic to find anomalies.
beats.title: Supervised vs Unsupervised Workflows
beats.visualDirection: Contrast two flow diagrams: one showing labeled data feeding a model, the other showing unlabeled data feeding a clustering algorithm.

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, which can invalidate results in security tool development.
beats.example: Scaling features using only training set statistics prevents test data information from contaminating the model's evaluation.
beats.title: Data Preprocessing and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Show a pipeline graphic with a 'Fit on Training Data' step and a 'Transform Training and Test' step, highlighting the boundary.

beats.claim: Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently across training and evaluation phases.
beats.example: A scikit-learn pipeline ensures that the same normalization and feature selection steps are applied to both training and test data for fair evaluation.
beats.title: Pipelines and Consistent Transformations
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a single pipeline block containing preprocessing steps followed by an estimator, with arrows showing consistent data flow.

beats.claim: Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits, and evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors.
beats.example: K-fold cross-validation ensures robust performance estimates, while precision and recall are chosen based on the cost of false positives versus false negatives in intrusion detection.
beats.title: Cross-Validation and Evaluation Metrics
beats.visualDirection: Display a k-fold cross-validation diagram with data splits and a table comparing metric selection to error cost scenarios.

beats.claim: Durable concepts and problem-solving methods require checking robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness before deploying intelligent security tools.
beats.example: A deployment checklist verifies that the AI model's robustness against distribution shift, privacy safeguards, security controls, transparency reports, and fairness audits are all documented.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with five checkboxes labeled 'Robustness', 'Privacy', 'Security', 'Transparency', and 'Fairness' alongside brief validation criteria.
